scenario.context: A company runs a customer portal on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances are distributed across two Availability Zones. The application stores transactional data in a self-managed relational database on one EC2 instance.
scenario.current_state: The web tier can continue operating after an instance failure, but a database host failure causes a prolonged outage while administrators restore a backup.
scenario.problem: The company needs automatic database failover across Availability Zones.

constraints.text: Tolerate the failure of one Availability Zone
Minimize database administration and failover work

stem: Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Move the database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment and update the application to use the database endpoint
Create an Amazon RDS read replica in another Availability Zone and direct all writes to the read replica after a failure
Run a second self-managed database on Amazon EC2 and create custom scripts to detect failures and promote the secondary
Store relational database files in an Amazon S3 bucket so that a replacement EC2 instance can mount them after a failure

explanation.summary: An Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment provides managed synchronous standby capacity and automatic failover while preserving a relational database interface and reducing administration.

option_analysis.A: RDS Multi-AZ is designed for managed high availability and automatic failover across Availability Zones.
option_analysis.B: A standard read replica is primarily a read-scaling mechanism and is not the direct managed automatic-failover solution described by the requirements.
option_analysis.C: A custom EC2-based replication and promotion design can be made to work but conflicts with the requirement to minimize administration and failover work.
option_analysis.D: Amazon S3 is object storage and cannot be mounted as relational database block storage in the proposed design.

learning_points: Read replicas and Multi-AZ deployments solve different primary problems
A technically possible custom design can still be the wrong answer when operations must be minimized
